_readme: THE source of truth for every value the cleartext stack's languages must agree on.
Above every generation on purpose. `host-contracts-cleartext/v12` and `v13` each hold a TypeScript
copy and a Solidity copy of these values, and until this file existed the four copies were only kept
in step by a naming convention and a test. This is the one place a value is DECIDED; the copies are
faces of it. See host-contracts-cleartext/RULES.md rule 23.
Why JSON and not TypeScript. Solidity cannot read a `.ts` module, and neither can a shell script, a
Rust crate, or a CI job that wants a chain id without installing a toolchain. Every language in this
repo can read JSON, and the emitted copies stay checked in — so an operator running `forge script`
against a testnet from an unbuilt checkout is never blocked on a generator having run.
## The shape of an entry
value      the value, as a string in every case — including integers. JSON numbers are IEEE doubles,
so a uint256 would silently lose precision on the way through a parser; a decimal string
cannot. Nothing here is fractional: every numeric value is a non-negative integer, and
there is no floating point anywhere in this file by construction.
alias      present instead of `value` when the constant is defined as another one. Both faces emit
the alias, not a repeat, so the two can never drift apart.
ts         the MINIMAL TypeScript type that holds the value exactly. A face may widen it — a uint
that fits a `number` also fits a `bigint`, so emitting `100733346448153n` where this says
`number` is fine. The reverse is not: a value that needs a `bigint` cannot be narrowed to
a `number` without losing digits, so `bigint` here is a floor and the check enforces it.
solidity   the Solidity type the mirror declares. Also what tells a consumer how to compare the
value: `address` case-insensitively, `string` exactly, `uint*` numerically.
formula    for a derived value, the expression it comes from — see below.
note       why the value is what it is. Required on every entry, and checked.
## Why a derived value records its formula
Three of these are keccak-derived, and the string being hashed is the real decision — the hex is only
what it hashes to. Recording only the hex makes the value unverifiable: a mistyped digit looks exactly
like a correct one, survives review, and then every copy of it agrees with every other. The formula is
written in Solidity syntax and is EVALUATED by the check, not merely displayed, so it cannot become a
comment that stopped being true. The preimage is not recorded separately: it is already in the formula,
and a second copy of a value is the thing this whole file exists to prevent.
## Exactness
Key order is declaration order, and emitters preserve it. It is load-bearing for `alias` entries, which
must be emitted after the constant they alias.
Values are copied, never tidied. The mnemonic paths end in `/` because forge's `vm.deriveKey(mnemonic,
path, index)` derives at `{path}{index}` by plain concatenation — a path written `m/44'/60'/0'/2`
silently derives `m/44'/60'/0'/20` for index 0. That is a valid path, a real key and an entirely wrong
signer set, and nothing else in a run notices: the stack deploys, verifies against itself, and fails
only when the js-sdk relayer arrives with keys at the documented path.

_note: The two generations use this set IDENTICALLY — `diff v13/internal/cleartext-config.ts
v12/internal/cleartext-config.ts` is empty today, which is why there is no per-generation section
here. That is a fact about today, not a design guarantee. Should a generation ever need a different
value, add an explicit `overrides` block keyed by generation rather than forking a copy: a forked
copy is indistinguishable from drift, which is the entire failure this file exists to end.

emittedTo._note: Every file that must agree with this one. RULES.md rule 23 requires names verbatim.

CLEARTEXT_GATEWAY_CHAIN_ID.note: A cheat-code chain id: chosen by hashing a name so it cannot collide with a real network by accident, and so anyone can reproduce it from the string alone. Truncated to 48 bits because a chain id has to fit where chain ids are stored, and 2^48 is far above any real one while still being nowhere near a plausible typo of one. `ts` is `number` because the value fits a double exactly; the emitted faces currently widen it to `bigint`, which this permits.

CLEARTEXT_RELAYER_URL.note: Deliberately a `.foo` TLD, which cannot be registered. A cleartext stack has no relayer to talk to, so the URL exists only to be well-formed; pointing it at an unregistrable name means a client that ignores the cleartext path and actually dials it fails to resolve rather than reaching somebody's real host.

CLEARTEXT_INPUT_VERIFICATION_ADDRESS.note: Where the gateway's input-verification contract is *said* to live. Nothing is ever deployed there — the address is a name the cleartext path can carry in place of a real one. Hashed rather than picked so it cannot collide with a deployed contract on any chain, and so it is reproducible from the string. Stored EIP-55 checksummed because Solidity REJECTS a hex address literal containing letters unless it is (error 9429), while TypeScript does not care — so the checksummed spelling is the one both faces can use verbatim.

CLEARTEXT_DECRYPTION_ADDRESS.note: The same idea as the input-verification address, for the gateway's decryption contract: a hashed placeholder, never deployed, reproducible from its preimage, and checksummed for Solidity's sake.

CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSOR_COUNT.note: How many coprocessor signers the stack registers on `InputVerifier`, and therefore how many keys are derived from the coprocessor HD path. Four rather than one because the multi-signer code paths are what a consumer exercises against a real deployment, and a stack with a single signer would let a bug in them pass unnoticed.

CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSOR_THRESHOLD.note: Equal to the count, not a majority. A cleartext stack has no real threshold cryptography whose partial failure it needs to tolerate, so requiring every signer keeps a missing or wrong one a loud failure instead of something the threshold silently absorbs.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODE_COUNT.note: How many KMS nodes the stack registers. In v13 it is also the length of every per-node metadata array `ProtocolConfig` stores — signer, tx-sender, IP address, storage URL — and every KMS threshold equals it, for the reason `CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSOR_THRESHOLD` gives.

CLEARTEXT_HCU_CAP_PER_BLOCK.note: Effectively uncapped, and uint48 max specifically because that is the width `HCULimit` stores the figure in — the largest value the field can hold, so the cap can never be the thing a test hits. The cleartext stack does no FHE work, so a real per-block HCU budget would only ever be an artificial limit.

CLEARTEXT_MAX_HCU_DEPTH_PER_TX.note: Kept at the protocol's real default rather than raised to the uint48 maximum like the per-block cap. Depth bounds how far a single transaction can chain dependent operations, and that limit is one a consumer can legitimately hit in cleartext just as in FHE — so leaving it realistic means a contract that would exceed it on a real stack also fails here, rather than passing and failing later.

CLEARTEXT_MAX_HCU_PER_TX.note: The per-transaction total, at the protocol's real default for the same reason as the depth limit: four times the depth bound, so a wide transaction is allowed more total work than a deep one.

FHEVM_MNEMONIC.value: test test test test test test test future home engine virtual motion
FHEVM_MNEMONIC.note: Published on purpose, and NOT the deploy mnemonic — a different string with a different job. This one is what makes a cleartext stack SDK-compatible: the js-sdk cleartext relayer derives its keys from it at the paths below and looks a signer up by the address they produce. Seed a different set and every other check still passes — the stack deploys, verifies against itself, and fails only when the relayer arrives. It is also why the stack is testnet-only: on mainnet these are keys everyone has.

CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSORS_MNEMONIC.note: An alias rather than a repeat, in both emitted faces. The three pools share one mnemonic today and are separated only by HD path; naming each one anyway lets a future generation give a pool its own mnemonic without touching a single call site.

CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSORS_MNEMONIC_PATH.note: The HD branch the coprocessor signer pool derives from. Its own branch, so the coprocessor and KMS pools can never overlap however either count changes. The trailing `/` is part of the value: `vm.deriveKey(mnemonic, path, index)` concatenates, so dropping it derives at `m/44'/60'/0'/2<index>` — real keys at a wrong path.

CLEARTEXT_COPROCESSORS_MNEMONIC_INDEX.note: The first index of the pool, which occupies `INDEX` through `INDEX + COUNT - 1`. Declared but currently read by nothing: `internal/generateSigners.ts` and `internal/generateLocalHostBytecode.ts` both start at 0 implicitly, so changing this today would have no effect. Recorded anyway because it is the value those two would have to consult, and having it named is what makes that a small change rather than a search. `uint32` on the Solidity side because that is what `vm.deriveKey`'s index parameter takes.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODES_MNEMONIC_PATH.note: The HD branch the KMS signing keys derive from — the set registered on `KMSVerifier` in v12 and on `ProtocolConfig` in v13. A branch of its own, distinct from both the coprocessors' and the tx-senders'. Trailing `/` load-bearing, as above.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODES_MNEMONIC_INDEX.note: First index of the KMS signing pool. Declared and currently unread, exactly as the coprocessors' index is.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODES_TX_SENDER_MNEMONIC_P.note: A pool distinct from the KMS signing keys, on its own branch. v13's `ProtocolConfig` records a tx-sender per node alongside that node's signer, and they are deliberately different keys: the address that submits a transaction is not the address that signed the payload. Trailing `/` load-bearing, as above.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODES_TX_SENDER_MNEMONIC_I.note: First index of the KMS tx-sender pool. Declared and currently unread, exactly as the other two indexes are.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODE_IP_ADDRESS_PREFIX.note: Node i gets `${prefix}${i + 1}` — so 127.0.0.1 through 127.0.0.4 — in both `pkg/ts/constants.ts` and `internal/generateLocalHostBytecode.ts`. Loopback deliberately: the per-node metadata v13's `ProtocolConfig` stores has to be well-formed, and must not name anything reachable. Note the one-based suffix, which is why the prefix ends at the final dot rather than including a digit.

CLEARTEXT_KMS_NODE_STORAGE_URL_PREFIX.note: Node i gets `${prefix}${i + 1}`, one-based like the IP prefix and built in the same two places. A plausible-looking s3 URL for a bucket that does not exist: `ProtocolConfig` only stores the string, so what matters is that it has the right shape and points nowhere.

_note: The fixed local-deploy addresses, and the recipe that produces them (RULES.md rules 15 and 17).
Separate from `constants` above because this block is NOT mirrored into FhevmCleartextConfig.sol. Its
faces are `<gen>/internal/constants.ts` and the GENERATED
`<gen>/pkg/forge/src/_internal/LocalHostAddresses.sol`, so the names here are those files' names, not
new ones — including `MNEMONIC`, which is deliberately kept even though it reads ambiguously next to
`FHEVM_MNEMONIC` in `constants`. The ambiguity is real and both files warn about it: two different
mnemonics with two different jobs, and swapping them produces a stack whose addresses look right and
whose signatures never verify. Renaming one here would hide that from a grep instead of fixing it.
These addresses are not ours to choose. `library-solidity/config/ZamaConfig.sol` returns three of them
from `_getLocalConfig()` on chain id 31337, and dApps INHERIT that library — so the literals are
compiled into consumer bytecode and cannot be reconfigured afterwards. A default local deploy landing
anywhere else leaves every such dApp calling addresses that hold no code.
Every address is `CREATE(DEPLOYER_ADDRESS, nonce)`, which is why they are recorded WITH their nonces
rather than as a bare list: the address is a function of the position, nothing else.
## primary and secondary
The nonce table is split in two, and the line is not editorial — it is the one the code already draws,
between `HOST_NONCE_OFFSET` and the entries positioned against `HOST_NONCE_COUNT` in
`<gen>/pkg/ts/addresses.ts`:
primary    the protocol stack proper — the two empty-proxy implementations plus every contract in
the `FhevmAddresses` type. These are upstream fhevm contracts, and this block is the one
that changes shape between generations: v13 adds `ProtocolConfig` and `KMSGeneration`.
secondary  everything positioned AFTER the primary block: the two cleartext-only contracts
(`CleartextAddresses`) and `PauserSet`. The same three roles in the same order in every
generation — only the nonce they start at moves.
That is the whole mechanism behind the divergence worth knowing about. v12 and v13 agree up to nonce 6
because their primary blocks agree that far; v13's primary block is two nonces LONGER, so its entire
secondary block shifts by two. `0x44aA028f…` is therefore `PROTOCOL_CONFIG_ADDRESS` (primary) in v13
and `CLEARTEXT_ARITHMETIC_ADDRESS` (secondary) in v12 — the same address, a different contract, and not
even the same category. Reading a role out of the wrong generation's table is silent, which is what the
per-generation split prevents; splitting each table into the two categories is what makes the reason
legible instead of a coincidence of numbering.
`test/cleartext-config-mirror.test.ts` re-derives all of it — the deployer from the mnemonic, then
every address from `CREATE(deployer, nonce)` — and compares the generated Solidity against the result.
Recomputing rather than transcribing is the point: a wrong hex digit here would otherwise be copied
into the generated file and agree with itself.

chainId.note: The chain id `ZamaConfig._getLocalConfig()` branches on, i.e. anvil's default. Not a value we picked; it is the condition under which a dApp compiled against ZamaConfig expects this exact address set.

MNEMONIC.value: adapt mosquito move limb mobile illegal tree voyage juice mosquito burger raise father hope layer
MNEMONIC.note: The DEPLOY mnemonic — it produces the deployer account, and through it every stack address. Not `FHEVM_MNEMONIC`, which derives the KMS and coprocessor signer pools. Named `MNEMONIC` because that is what `internal/constants.ts` calls it.

DEPLOYER_ADDRESS_INDEX.note: Account index of the deployer within MNEMONIC, at HD path `m/44'/60'/0'/0/5`. Load-bearing: together with a start nonce of 0 it is what makes the deploy land on the addresses ZamaConfig compiles into consumers. Changing it moves the entire stack.

DEPLOYER_ADDRESS.derivation: the account at m/44'/60'/0'/0/{DEPLOYER_ADDRESS_INDEX} of MNEMONIC
DEPLOYER_ADDRESS.note: Recorded as well as derived so a consumer that only wants the address does not need an HD wallet implementation. The check re-derives it, so the two cannot part company.

DEPLOYER_START_NONCE.note: The deployer must have sent NOTHING when the sequence begins. Part of the address derivation rather than a precondition to be polite about: `CREATE(deployer, nonce)` means a deployer at any other nonce produces a different stack. Emitted into LocalHostAddresses.sol so a consumer can assert it rather than discover it.

0.13.0._note: PROXY_COUNT is the arity of the ACLOwner ops array; ADDRESSED_NONCE_COUNT is one past the last nonce any baked-in address depends on — the first nonce a deploy may spend freely. Both are generated, never hand-written, and both change with the generation.

0.12.0._note: Two fewer proxies and two fewer nonces than v13: this generation has no ProtocolConfig and no KMSGeneration. Everything from nonce 7 on therefore names a different contract than v13's table does at the same nonce.
